epics.title: Foundation, contracts, and reproducibility
epics.outcome: Explain the architecture, freeze a verified baseline, and start a buildable .NET/Aspire skeleton.
epics.exit_criteria: A fresh checkout restores, builds, and starts the skeleton; the API and synthetic data contracts are documented.

epics.title: Observable .NET support workflow
epics.outcome: Implement the read-only Chapter 7 support path with guarded tools, routing, DevUI, and telemetry.
epics.exit_criteria: Demonstrate read-only orders, billing, and technical requests with correlated workflow/model/tool telemetry; mutating tools remain unregistered until E03.

epics.title: Conversations, approvals, and streaming
epics.outcome: Preserve conversation state and safely pause/resume side-effecting work.
epics.exit_criteria: Demonstrate isolated follow-ups, bound approval/rejection for all simulated writes, restart/resume, duplicate protection, and the shared streaming terminal outcomes.

epics.title: Safety, reliability, and measurement
epics.outcome: Strengthen and verify established business boundaries, bound failures, and measure behavior/resource use.
epics.exit_criteria: Show unauthorized access rejection, bounded failure handling, and a baseline evaluation with honest cost/quality limits.

epics.title: Python implementation and behavioral parity
epics.outcome: Rebuild the complete behavior idiomatically in Python and compare SDK choices.
epics.exit_criteria: Both backends pass the same deterministic contracts, ownership, approval, durable-state, streaming, resilience, and injection-boundary scenarios with isolated state and comparable telemetry.

epics.title: One frontend for both implementations
epics.outcome: Verify browser compatibility with the established backend contract and add one shared frontend.
epics.exit_criteria: Select a backend when starting a conversation, chat, approve/reject an operation, and diagnose a failure.

epics.title: Engineering evidence and interview readiness
epics.outcome: Demonstrate the system, defend decisions, and state its operational limits.
epics.exit_criteria: Complete a fault demonstration, publish a reproducible runbook, and answer a recorded or written mock interview.

tickets.title: Audit Chapter 7 and record a verified version baseline
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Recheck runtime support and compatible released MAF, provider, Aspire, hosting, and DevUI packages; record prerelease rationale and provider/model capabilities needed for tools and structured output.
Map both Chapter 7 request paths and confirm the static audit; distinguish hosted behavior from unused helper code.
Write docs/decisions/0001-version-baseline.md with candidate versions, checked source links, and explicit restore/build/import verification to perform at L03/L04 and L17.
acceptance: The decision separates observed release versions from a restored/tested dependency set, and selects a provider/model configuration without committing credentials.
Explain the actual hosted security/refund path and one documentation/source disagreement; the decision names how fake mode and opt-in live checks will be used.
learning_outcomes: Separate framework concepts from provider/hosting integrations.
Read migration notes and resolve stale course examples.
interview_questions: How do you establish that a tutorial is compatible with the SDK you selected?
Why can core be released while DevUI or hosting remains prerelease?
tickets.stretch: Find one additional assumption in the capstone and prove or disprove it from tagged source.
scope_exclusions: Installing or implementing the support system
Claiming compatibility from release numbers alone

tickets.title: Define shared support contracts and synthetic fixtures
tickets.source_note: The course contracts and tools illustrate domain behavior. The shared HTTP/streaming protocol, reset rules, and threat model are project additions.
implementation: Define the version-1 HTTP request/response, conversation, operation-status, approval, error, and planned streaming schemas in contracts/; decide the transport mapping now and record it in contracts/README.md.

Define one terminal transport outcome per turn: completed, awaiting_approval, failed, or cancelled. Awaiting approval is a pause, not a completed business action. Specify refresh/status lookup and how subsequent approval resumes work.
Seed synthetic customers, orders, refund/cancellation eligibility rules, and scenario inputs; define reset/isolation rules for each backend and evaluation run.
Draft trust boundaries and operation-risk rules in docs/threat-model.md. Preserve original user text beside derived fields and keep principal/ownership authority outside model arguments.
acceptance: Contract examples cover success, missing/unknown order, invalid route, forbidden access, approval denial, operation-status lookup, stream pause/error, and duplicate submission.

Schema checks reject invalid routes/ranges and incompatible envelopes. HTTP routes, event shapes, error codes, state ownership, and versioning rules are documented before either backend implements them.
Fixtures contain two synthetic customers with distinct orders and eligibility outcomes; each backend/run can reset its own mutable state without resetting the other.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish schema validity, factual validity, and business authorization.
Design a language-neutral observable contract.
Separate transport outcomes from business-operation state and evolve a shared contract compatibly.
interview_questions: Why does structured output not guarantee a correct or authorized operation?
What should be shared between equivalent C# and Python implementations?
tickets.stretch: Add an ambiguous request and describe the expected clarification behavior.

tickets.title: Scaffold .NET support API and C# Aspire AppHost
tickets.source_note: Chapter 7 composition roots are comparison points; Aspire, fake-mode startup, and the development identity boundary are project additions.
implementation: Create the C# AppHost and ASP.NET Core skeleton, commit the selected SDK/direct package versions, and document prerequisites; keep agent behavior for L05.
Add health/configuration handling with an explicit offline/fake mode that starts without provider credentials; validate required credentials only when live mode is selected.
Establish a fixed server-owned development principal and a trusted test-host identity injection point. Do not accept a model-supplied identity or an arbitrary customer header as authority.
Launch the API through Aspire with local development endpoints and document service versus agent-workflow responsibilities.
acceptance: A clean checkout restores/builds and starts the fake-mode API through AppHost without a model key or billable request; health is visible.
Selecting live mode with incomplete configuration fails clearly without exposing secrets. The test host can exercise two principals without enabling client identity spoofing.
learning_outcomes: Separate process orchestration from agent workflow orchestration.
Understand composition roots, configuration, and health.
Establish offline startup and a trusted development identity before agents can access records.
interview_questions: What does Aspire manage, and what remains the application's responsibility?
Where should provider credentials and service endpoints be configured?
tickets.stretch: Change the local service port and prove the AppHost-provided endpoint still works.

tickets.title: Add reproducible builds and meaningful offline CI
tickets.source_note: The course dependency manifest motivates reproducibility; CI is an extension beyond the capstone.
implementation: Enable locked restore and commit compatible dependency locks for the skeleton introduced in L03; record runtime/SDK selection already made there.
Extend CI to build the AppHost/API and run meaningful contract/configuration/identity-boundary integration tests in fake mode.
Keep repository-checks as the stable always-reported required aggregate; every introduced language check must feed it. Document offline tests and explicit live verification separately.
Configure dependency updates for the introduced NuGet manifests; keep network-backed advisory checks separate from deterministic fake-model tests.
acceptance: A fresh locked restore/build/test succeeds without provider credentials and fails for deliberate schema/configuration/identity-boundary regressions.
The required repository-checks aggregate reports on every PR and fails if a mandatory child check fails; skipped language paths cannot hide required failures or leave a permanently pending check.
learning_outcomes: Reproducibility and dependency locking.
Design CI around real failure modes and required-check behavior.
interview_questions: How do you test an agent application without paying for model calls on every PR?
Why can path-filtered required workflows block merges?
tickets.stretch: Reproduce a failed CI check locally from the documented command.
scope_exclusions: Python/frontend builds before their projects exist

tickets.title: Build the first .NET order-status agent and DevUI
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Create one support agent and an order-status tool backed by fixture services; enforce order ownership using the trusted principal established in L03.
Use the L02 version-1 contract for the support API and expose the same underlying behavior through development-only DevUI.
Add a controllable fake model/client at the provider boundary, deterministic tool/host tests, and a separately invoked bounded live smoke check.
acceptance: Known/unknown orders and missing IDs produce the specified result or clarification. Cross-customer queries are denied by the service regardless of model arguments.
DevUI discovers the agent; API/DevUI entry points use the same service guards. Tool calls can be inspected in DevUI; full OTLP verification belongs to L06.
learning_outcomes: Understand the model/tool invocation loop.
Keep agent construction reusable across API and development tooling.
interview_questions: When should a model call a tool rather than answer from its prompt?
How does DevUI relate to your application API?
tickets.stretch: Remove the order ID and require a clarification without calling the lookup tool.

tickets.title: Export traces, metrics, and structured logs to Aspire
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Instrument HTTP, agent/model, and tool operations with correlated spans and sanitized structured logs; configure explicit trace, metric, and log export to Aspire.
Record request/error counts and latency with bounded labels such as route, tool, and outcome. Put conversation/operation identifiers in appropriate traces/logs, never unbounded metric labels.
Keep sensitive capture opt-in and choose instrumentation ownership to avoid duplicate providers, exporters, or usage accounting. L07 adds workflow spans when routing exists.
acceptance: A fake-mode success and failure appear in Aspire with correlated logs, useful error status, and actual metric samples; a live run is an optional separate check.
Document listened-to sources/meters, service/version identity, and which layer owns each signal. Nested agent/model spans remain distinguishable; one usage observation is not charged twice.
learning_outcomes: Separate instrumentation, providers, exporters, and the telemetry backend.
Distinguish traces, logs, counters, and distributions.
interview_questions: Why does seeing a trace not prove metrics are configured?
How do you correlate a request while avoiding sensitive data in telemetry?
tickets.stretch: Break the OTLP endpoint and explain the failure from application/exporter diagnostics.
scope_exclusions: Unbounded metric labels or always-on sensitive capture

tickets.title: Implement validated triage and deterministic routing
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Produce and validate typed triage with allowed routes, bounded fields, and a controlled invalid/ambiguous fallback; do not treat generated confidence as calibrated correctness.
Build conditional workflow routing. Keep the existing orders path working; use clearly identified test doubles/placeholders for billing/technical until L08.
Pass original request plus validated fields and trusted context to executors; extend the L06 telemetry chain with workflow/executor spans using the selected release's names.
acceptance: Deterministic route tests cover orders, billing, and technical without claiming unimplemented specialists are operational; the orders path remains end to end.
Malformed JSON, unknown category, and missing required information lead to a defined error/fallback/clarification. A trace connects routing to its selected executor.
learning_outcomes: Use LLM classification inside deterministic control flow.
Understand generated confidence is not calibrated correctness.
interview_questions: What should be deterministic in an agent workflow?
How would you detect and improve poor routing?
tickets.stretch: Add an out-of-domain request without introducing another specialist.
scope_exclusions: Claiming billing/technical placeholders are complete agents

tickets.title: Complete read-only .NET billing and technical specialists
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Replace the billing/technical placeholders from L07 with read-only invoice/payment-history and knowledge-search tools over customer-scoped fixture services.
Give each specialist only its required tools and preserve order/invoice/article identifiers and the original request context in factual responses.

Add invoice, knowledge-search, unknown-record, and unresolved-issue scenarios. An unresolved issue may offer escalation; actual ticket creation, refunds, and cancellations are introduced with approval in L10.
acceptance: Read-only requests in all three domains run through the version-1 support path and appear in the workflow trace.
No mutating tool is registered by this ticket. Failed searches produce an honest unresolved/handoff suggestion; cross-customer data access is denied.
learning_outcomes: Design scoped capabilities and factual tool-backed answers.
Understand single-agent versus specialist tradeoffs.
interview_questions: When do specialist agents justify additional model calls?
How do you prevent a specialist from exceeding its intended capabilities?
tickets.stretch: Compare one request with a single-agent baseline and record the call-count tradeoff.

tickets.title: Add per-conversation sessions and preserve context
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Map version-1 conversation IDs to per-conversation routing/specialist sessions owned by the trusted development principal.
Support follow-ups with original messages and validated order/customer state; preserve the appropriate native session across turns rather than rebuilding a stateless specialist call.
Define a bounded history policy and serialize or reject competing turns on the same conversation while allowing separate conversations to proceed.
acceptance: An order follow-up works without repeating its ID and routes correctly using established context.
Two principals/conversations have isolated state, an unauthorized conversation lookup is denied, and concurrent turns have a documented deterministic policy. Durable restart comes in L11.
learning_outcomes: Separate agent object lifetime from conversation state.
Understand history, session state, and context limits.
interview_questions: Can a reusable agent be shared while conversations remain isolated?
What belongs in conversation history versus application state?
tickets.stretch: Simulate simultaneous requests to one conversation and define the conflict policy.

tickets.title: Require bound approval for simulated support mutations
tickets.source_note: Use course refund/cancellation/ticket tools as domain examples. This baseline deliberately approval-gates every simulated write; the course does not provide the complete host-boundary and persistence design.
implementation: Introduce simulated refund, cancellation, and support-ticket creation tools over in-memory fixture state; use the native framework approval mechanism for all three in this learning baseline.

Adapt native pending requests/responses to the L02 approval and operation-status contract, binding principal, conversation, operation identity, tool, and exact arguments. Rejection must not trigger an immediate repeat request.
Enforce eligibility and customer access inside services using the L03/L05/L09 trusted boundaries; remove model-supplied confirmation authority. Durable storage/idempotency is the next ticket.
acceptance: For refund, cancellation, and ticket creation: absent/denied approval produces zero mutation, and an approved eligible operation changes simulated state and returns its factual result.
Changed arguments, wrong operation, wrong principal/conversation, and ineligible actions cannot reuse approval. Tests prove the native approval gate and service authorization both apply.
learning_outcomes: Separate user intent, human approval, and business authorization.
Understand the approval pause/resume lifecycle.
interview_questions: Why is a customerConfirmed argument supplied by the model insufficient?
What data must an approval be bound to?
tickets.stretch: Reject an action and verify the agent does not immediately repeat the same request.

tickets.title: Persist pending approvals and prevent duplicate operations
tickets.source_note: The course refund runner illustrates approval flow, not durable restart/resume or idempotency.
implementation: Choose a supported local durable store and document session serialization versus workflow checkpoint responsibilities in docs/decisions/0003-state-and-idempotency.md.

Persist pending approvals/expiry, operation status, required native session/checkpoint state, and stable workflow/agent identities. Protect restore/status access using the owning principal and conversation.
Use a durable operation key plus atomic simulated business-state/operation-record changes for refunds, cancellations, and ticket creation; isolate state by backend and evaluation run.
acceptance: Restart between request and approval, restore the matching native state, and resume the intended operation; wrong-owner, expired, rejected, or mismatched operations do not execute.
Duplicate submission/approval and a crash after the simulated commit but before response delivery produce one mutation and a retrievable final status for each write type.
Document the atomic local-store guarantee and why it does not imply exactly-once execution against an arbitrary external provider.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish workflow durability from side-effect idempotency.
Understand restart/replay and stable identities.
interview_questions: Does checkpointing guarantee exactly-once external side effects?
What state must survive an approval wait and process restart?
tickets.stretch: Crash immediately after the fake refund commits and before the response is sent.
scope_exclusions: Exactly-once guarantees for arbitrary external providers

tickets.title: Implement streaming, cancellation, and terminal events
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Implement L02's chosen streaming transport and event schema for progress/deltas plus exactly one terminal outcome per connected turn: completed, awaiting_approval, failed, or cancelled.
Persist pending/final operation status so a new request or status lookup can resolve a disconnected approval/write; do not promise replay of model tokens unless separately implemented.
Propagate cooperative cancellation to SDK/tool work, stop launching new work, and choose buffered versus incremental output validation explicitly; measure first-output and full-response latency.
acceptance: A successful, paused, failed, and cancelled turn each follow the same event contract; a pause is not reported as successful business completion, and partial structured data never drives routing.

Disconnect before a write leaves no new mutation; disconnect/cancellation after a committed write preserves factual status and duplicate protection. The application does not claim cancellation rolls back an already committed operation.
learning_outcomes: Understand asynchronous streaming and cancellation propagation.
Recognize filtering/latency tradeoffs.
interview_questions: How does transport streaming differ from actual model-token streaming?
How do you handle an error after an HTTP stream has begun?
What should happen when the client cancels after a refund has already committed?
tickets.stretch: Disconnect the client while a slow tool runs and inspect the trace.
scope_exclusions: Rollback of a committed action on disconnect

tickets.title: Verify customer access and conversation ownership boundaries
tickets.source_note: Course tools expose synthetic records without the complete ownership model. This ticket strengthens and verifies earlier guards; it does not postpone basic authorization until this point.
implementation: Consolidate and adversarially verify the trusted development-identity and ownership guards already introduced in L03/L05/L09/L10/L11.
Exercise every record read, conversation lookup, status lookup, approval, and mutation under both synthetic principals; include API and DevUI entry points.
Update docs/threat-model.md with identity provenance, tested boundaries, and the explicit gap between the local development principal and production authentication.
acceptance: A cross-customer matrix proves record, conversation, operation-status, approval, and mutation access is denied at the application/service boundary.
Model arguments, client customer headers, and guessed IDs cannot change the trusted principal. Tests cover all current entry points; the baseline makes no production-authentication claim.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish authentication, authorization, and model context.
Apply resource-level access controls to agent tools.
interview_questions: Where should authorization run in a tool-calling application?
Why does knowing an order ID not establish permission to access it?
tickets.stretch: Attempt cross-customer access through both the direct tool/service test and agent-facing API.
scope_exclusions: Introducing the first ownership guard this late
Claiming a development principal is production authentication

tickets.title: Validate tool boundaries and exercise prompt injection
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Strengthen validation of tool arguments and rendering/output boundaries; keep developer instructions separate from user and tool-result data.
Add direct and tool-result injection scenarios that attempt a cross-customer read, unauthorized write, or changed approved arguments.
Treat phrase filters as diagnostic heuristics and verify action/ownership/approval gates independently of whether the model detects an attack; extend the threat model.
acceptance: The adversarial fixture matrix demonstrates that tested unauthorized/cross-customer/unapproved actions are rejected even when the fake model attempts them.
Document false positives, bypass examples, and coverage limits. Do not claim complete prompt-injection prevention; output handling and default telemetry avoid exposing sensitive test data.
learning_outcomes: Understand direct versus indirect prompt injection.
Separate detection heuristics from enforceable business controls.
interview_questions: Why are regex filters insufficient for prompt injection?
What happens when an LLM follows an instruction embedded in a tool result?
tickets.stretch: Create a paraphrased attack that bypasses the course phrase matcher and prove the operation gate still holds.
scope_exclusions: Experimental security middleware as a cross-language requirement

tickets.title: Add bounded timeouts, retries, and graceful failure
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Set model/tool timeouts, maximum tool/agent steps, output limits, and per-turn budgets; preserve L12's cancellation behavior.

Inventory retries in the provider SDK, HTTP client, and application; assign one retry owner per layer and a bounded end-to-end attempt budget. Retry only eligible operations and use L11 operation state for writes.
Represent rate limits, unavailable tools/providers, invalid output, and exhausted budgets with version-1 error/terminal outcomes and a trace reference; respect provider retry hints where applicable.
acceptance: Deterministic transient, permanent, timeout, rate-limit, and loop-budget faults have bounded attempts/latency and the specified safe outcome.
Layered retries cannot multiply beyond the documented budget; cancellation stops new attempts and retrying a write cannot repeat its committed mutation.
learning_outcomes: Classify transient failures versus invalid requests.
Understand resilience costs and retry amplification.
interview_questions: Which operations are safe to retry and why?
How can retries increase latency and model spend?
tickets.stretch: Combine a transient failure with cancellation and show the work stops.

tickets.title: Establish behavioral, latency, and usage baselines
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Create the endpoint-configurable evaluation runner and at least 20 shared scenarios for reads, routing, ambiguity, ownership, all write approvals, restart, cancellation, and failures.
Run the .NET baseline now. Keep the same runner/fixtures ready for Python in L21, but do not claim Python parity before it exists. Reset only the selected backend/run state.

Report routing/tool/action invariants, latency, and provider-reported usage. Mark unavailable usage unknown, distinguish cached-token categories where reported, and label rate-based cost estimates separately from billed cost.
Separate deterministic fake-mode CI gates from opt-in repeated live runs; record configuration, model/deployment, sample count, thresholds, and limitations.
acceptance: A deliberately incorrect route, missing ownership check, or duplicate write fails the deterministic runner, which emits machine-readable and human-readable results.
The recorded baseline identifies .NET as its target; unavailable usage is not zero and nested telemetry is not double-counted. Natural-language wording is not compared by exact equality.
learning_outcomes: Separate correctness evaluations from operational metrics.
Understand variability, sample size, and cost estimation.
interview_questions: How would you evaluate an agent beyond answer quality?
Why is self-reported model confidence not a substitute for labelled evaluation?
tickets.stretch: Change one prompt and compare behavior/cost with an unchanged evaluation set.
scope_exclusions: Treating estimated cost as billing or unknown usage as zero

tickets.title: Scaffold Python packaging, health, and Aspire integration
tickets.source_note: The Python course setup is a reference for configuration; Aspire packaging and CI are extensions.
implementation: Create src/python/ with pyproject.toml/uv.lock, a host/configuration shell, and the same fixed server-owned development-principal/test-host boundary as .NET.
Support fake-mode startup without credentials, live-mode configuration validation, health, and independent local execution; register the Python process in the C# AppHost.
Add locked sync/import/lint/configuration tests to the stable required CI aggregate; keep mutable state separate and document Python client/credential cleanup ownership.
Extend dependency update coverage for the actual Python manifest/lock format and select a supported updater configuration.
acceptance: Both hosts start through AppHost; the Python host also runs independently without provider secrets or billable calls in fake mode.
Locked environment/import/configuration checks pass and fail on a deliberate config/identity-boundary regression; code cannot import a C# helper to obtain its telemetry or authorization behavior.
learning_outcomes: Understand Python package/import structure and environment locking.
Compare hosting/configuration conventions across languages.
Port the trusted host boundary and resource lifecycle without treating model arguments as identity.
interview_questions: What is the role of uv.lock versus pyproject.toml?
How does Aspire launch a Python service while its logic stays independent?
tickets.stretch: Launch only Python outside Aspire using the documented configuration.
scope_exclusions: Reusing a C# library as Python application logic

tickets.title: Implement Python read-only agents, tools, and triage
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Port L05/L07/L08's read-only orders, billing, and technical behavior using idiomatic Python types, validated models, workflow executors, and a controllable fake client.
Enforce principal-scoped record access, preserve original requests/validated fields, and use the unchanged version-1 contract and shared fixtures.
Expose development-only Python DevUI for agent/workflow inspection; register no mutating tools until L19 implements the approval gate.
acceptance: The shared known/unknown/missing record and route checks pass; invalid output reaches the same controlled fallback and cross-customer reads are denied.
All read-only specialists are discoverable in DevUI; no mutating tool can run. Each entry point uses the same guarded services; Python OTLP verification belongs to L20.
learning_outcomes: Compare C# response types/executors with Python models/handlers.
Understand the common model/tool/workflow concepts.
interview_questions: Which differences are SDK conventions and which change observable behavior?
Where should Python validate model-generated values?
tickets.stretch: Implement an ambiguous routing scenario without consulting the C# code.
scope_exclusions: Weakening the shared schemas to fit the SDK

tickets.title: Implement Python sessions, approval persistence, and idempotency
tickets.source_note: Course always_require tools and executors illustrate the concept. This ticket ports the established .NET state/authorization/idempotency design; it is larger than a single new-concept exercise and should be worked in the three listed slices.
implementation: Port L09-L11's conversation isolation, pending approvals, durable restore/status lookup, and all three simulated write types with the same eligibility rules.
Bind native Python approval requests to the owning session and exact proposed operation; preserve that state across restart without using unbound approval responses.
Apply the .NET baseline's customer/service authorization, atomic local-store operation records, expiry policy, and backend/run namespaces; use idiomatic Python resource cleanup.
acceptance: Follow-up, same-conversation concurrency, approval denial/change/replay, wrong-owner status lookup, expiry, restart/resume, and every write type pass the same expected business invariants.
Duplicate approval/submission and a crash after commit yield one mutation and factual final status; restoration uses matching native state and stable identities.
learning_outcomes: Understand Python session-bound approval and durable state.
Separate language parity from line-by-line translation.
Prove the same authorization, durable-operation, and duplicate-submission invariants with native Python sessions.
interview_questions: How does the current Python SDK bind an approval to a pending request?
Why should session state be isolated even when an agent definition is reusable?
tickets.stretch: Attempt a replay from a second conversation and inspect the rejection.

tickets.title: Complete Python streaming, telemetry, and resilience
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Port L12's event/cancellation/operation-status behavior, preserving the same completed/awaiting_approval/failed/cancelled distinction and buffering policy.
Export traces/logs/metrics with explicit Python service identity and bounded labels; reconcile DevUI's sensitive-capture behavior and avoid duplicate provider/handler setup.
Port L14/L15's tested boundary-validation cases, model/tool/step/output budgets, retry ownership, failure envelopes, and secret-safe output handling.
acceptance: Python streaming, pause/resume, disconnect-after-commit, cancellation, timeout, rate-limit, step-budget, and injection-boundary checks match the .NET expected outcomes.
All three signals arrive in Aspire; first-output latency/buffering is measured, usage accounting is not duplicated, and resource-owning clients/credentials close at host shutdown.
learning_outcomes: Understand async streams and middleware buffering.
Compare .NET and Python telemetry configuration and lifecycle ownership.
Carry boundary checks and end-to-end retry/step budgets into the second SDK rather than relying on provider defaults.
interview_questions: Why can a streamed API still buffer the entire answer?
How do provider setup and logger propagation cause duplicate telemetry?
How can different provider defaults break cross-language retry or cancellation guarantees?
tickets.stretch: Toggle the safe development telemetry setting and verify exactly what changes.
scope_exclusions: Deferring Python security/retry behavior beyond parity
Shared global conversation state or duplicate telemetry setup

tickets.title: Run cross-language parity checks and document SDK decisions
tickets.source_note: Use the course files to understand the behavior; adapt the implementation to the selected release.
implementation: Run L16's unchanged endpoint-configurable deterministic suite against each backend with isolated/reset state; include identity, all writes, durable restore, streaming, retry budgets, and safe failures.

Classify differences as defects, internal SDK choices that preserve the contract, or measured live-model variability. Business/security contract violations must be fixed rather than accepted as SDK differences.

Write docs/decisions/0002-sdk-comparison.md covering tools, sessions/checkpoints, routing, approvals, cancellation, resource lifecycle, telemetry, and resilience; record package/provider/model settings.
acceptance: Both implementations pass the same deterministic contract/business/security gates in CI without credentials. Optional live comparisons report configuration, repetitions, and variance.
Equivalent routes/actions/state are required while prose may vary; every intentionally different internal SDK choice is documented and preserves the shared public contract.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate behavioral equivalence without requiring identical prose.
Defend idiomatic implementation choices.
interview_questions: How do you prove two probabilistic implementations meet one specification?
What differences would influence your choice of SDK for a team?
tickets.stretch: Demonstrate a defect in one backend that the shared suite detects.
scope_exclusions: Accepting business/security violations as SDK differences

tickets.title: Verify browser compatibility with the established API contract
tickets.source_note: Course hosting/approval behavior motivates the browser probes. L02 owns the API design; this ticket verifies browser compatibility rather than finalizing a new protocol after parity.
implementation: Use a minimal disposable browser probe to verify L02's existing version-1 contract after both backends pass L21; record browser-specific integration decisions without redefining backend behavior.
Verify conversation/backend binding, relative frontend API addressing via the server/dev proxy, stream decoding, pending-status lookup after refresh, and safe error rendering.
Keep backend aliases/endpoints server-controlled. Any discovered breaking contract change requires updating schemas, both adapters, and the shared evaluations before UI work proceeds.
acceptance: The same browser probes pass for chat, stream pause/error, approval/rejection, refreshed pending status, and disconnect recovery against either backend.
One conversation stays on its original backend; no provider key, arbitrary backend URL, or Aspire-internal service DNS name is required in browser code.
learning_outcomes: Design a frontend around asynchronous workflow state.
Distinguish developer tools from a product interface.
interview_questions: What does the browser need to render a paused workflow?
How do you keep sessions coherent when two equivalent backends exist?
tickets.stretch: Specify how a refreshed browser discovers a pending approval.
scope_exclusions: A complete frontend or product authentication

tickets.title: Build shared chat UI with backend selection
tickets.source_note: Course composition roots are comparison references; this UI is original project work.
implementation: Choose/document a modest frontend stack and implement chat plus backend-alias selection only when starting a new conversation.
Consume the existing contract to render progress, validated output, safe errors, and current backend; defer approval controls and refresh UX to L24.
Register the frontend in AppHost and configure relative API calls through its server/dev proxy using Aspire-provided backend URLs; keep provider credentials exclusively on backends.
Commit the frontend dependency lock, add its build/type/lint checks as appropriate to the chosen stack to the required aggregate, and configure dependency updates for its manifest.
acceptance: One UI completes order-status follow-ups against either backend with the same session semantics.
